readerTitle: Why the faster delivery got the worse review
caseNote: 실제 연구 (Oliver 1980 기대-불일치 이론, Parasuraman·Zeithaml·Berry 1985 서비스 갭 모델) + 가상 사례 (화물 운송사 두 곳, 소프트웨어 기능 출시 일정) · 수치는 모두 설명용
insight: 고객은 경험을 절대 기준이 아니라 자신이 기대한 것과 비교해 평가한다. 그래서 약속은 경험만큼 중요한 설계 대상이다.
misconception: 더 빠르고 더 좋게 해 주면 고객 만족은 저절로 올라간다.

sources.text: Oliver, R. L. (1980). A Cognitive Model of the Antecedents and Consequences of Satisfaction Decisions. Journal of Marketing Research, 17(4).
Parasuraman, A., Zeithaml, V. A., & Berry, L. L. (1985). A Conceptual Model of Service Quality and Its Implications for Future Research. Journal of Marketing, 49(4).
운송사와 소프트웨어 사례의 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 운송사 사례는 가상입니다. 계산: A사 약속 2일 − 실제 3일 = 1일 늦음, B사 약속 5일 − 실제 4일 = 1일 빠름. A사가 실제로는 1일 더 빨랐습니다(3일 vs 4일). 평점 수치는 지어내지 않았고 방향만 서술했습니다.
Oliver(1980)는 만족이 기대와 그 기대가 확인·불일치된 정도에 따라 결정된다는 기대-불일치 모델을 제시했습니다. 카드에서는 'experience minus expectation'으로 단순화했으니 표현이 과하지 않은지 확인하세요.
Parasuraman 외(1985)의 갭 모델은 고객이 기대한 서비스와 인식한 서비스의 차이를 서비스 품질로 봅니다. 기대의 원천(구전, 개인적 필요, 과거 경험, 기업 커뮤니케이션)이 논문 내용과 맞는지 확인하세요.

cards.title: Why the faster delivery got the worse review
body: Two freight companies move the same pallets on the same route. One gets them there in three days. The other takes four.
The slower one gets the happier customers. Nothing went wrong with its trucks. Something went right with one sentence it said before the trip.

image.label: Two delivery trucks, the slower one greeted with a smile
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 같은 도로를 달리는 화물 트럭 두 대. 앞선 트럭 도착지에는 팔짱 낀 창고 직원, 뒤따르는 트럭 도착지에는 엄지를 든 직원. 실제 운송사 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Which customer is happier?
body: Firm A promises delivery in 2 days. The pallets arrive in 3.
Firm B promises delivery in 5 days. The pallets arrive in 4.
Both customers fill in a short survey. Which one rates the delivery higher?

options.text: Firm A's customer. Three days beats four.
options.feedback: The goods did arrive sooner. But the customer planned around day two, so day three feels like a broken promise.

options.text: Firm B's customer. The pallets came early.
options.feedback: Right. The customer planned for day five, and day four felt like a gift. The next card shows why.

options.text: About the same. One day apart either way.
options.feedback: The gap is one day in both cases. But one gap points down and one points up, and customers feel the direction.

cards.title: Same gap, opposite sign.
body: Firm A was faster by a day. It was also late by a day. Firm B was slower, and early. The customer scored the gap, not the clock.

cards.title: Expectations vs experience
body: Customers don't judge what happened on its own. They judge it against what they **expected** to happen.
Satisfaction is roughly *experience minus expectation*. Beat the expectation and people feel pleased. Fall short and they feel let down, even when the result is objectively good.
Marketing researcher Richard Oliver described this in 1980 as *expectation disconfirmation*: satisfaction depends on whether reality confirms, beats or misses what people expected.

image.label: A scale weighing 'Expected' against 'Experienced'
image.brief: 저울 인포그래픽. 왼쪽 접시 "Expected", 오른쪽 접시 "Experienced". 오른쪽이 더 무거우면 웃는 얼굴, 가벼우면 실망한 얼굴이 아래에 표시됨.

cards.title: Where expectations come from.
body: Service researchers Parasuraman, Zeithaml and Berry described service quality as the gap between what customers expect and what they perceive. Those expectations are built before the customer ever meets you.
list: **Your price:** paying more raises the bar
**Past visits:** last time's free upgrade becomes this time's baseline
**Other people:** reviews and word of mouth
cards.callout: You control half of this list. Most businesses only manage the experience.

cards.title: Raising expectations has a cost.
body: A bold headline, a premium price or a generous one-off gesture all lift the bar. The next experience has to clear it.

Picture a restaurant that gives a regular a free dessert three visits in a row. On the fourth visit, the same great meal without dessert feels a little worse. Nothing changed in the kitchen. The expectation moved.
So every promise is a decision about how future experiences will be judged.

cards.title: Underpromising has limits too.
body: Customers choose you *before* they experience you, based on the promise. Quote ten days when rivals quote four, and you may never get the chance to delight anyone.
Padding also gets found out. Customers who always see early arrivals start expecting them, and your buffer disappears.
And early isn't always better. A warehouse with no space for pallets on day four may not thank you. The goal is an honest, reliable promise, not a low one.

cards.title: Now it's a software feature.
body: Your biggest client asks when a requested integration will ship. Your team usually ships work like this in 4 to 8 weeks.
What do you tell them?

options.text: "Four weeks." It's possible, and it keeps them excited.
options.feedback: You win a happy call today. But most outcomes land after week four, so you've set up a likely miss with your biggest client.

options.text: "Within eight weeks, with an update every two."
options.feedback: An honest outer date makes an earlier ship feel like a win, and regular updates keep expectations current as things change.

options.text: "No date yet. We'll tell you when it's live."
options.feedback: You avoid a broken promise. But the client fills the silence with their own guess, and that guess is usually sooner than yours.

cards.title: Customers grade you against your promise.
body: Manage the expectation as carefully as the experience. An honest promise you beat often wins more than a fast one you miss.
**Try it today:** pick one promise your business makes, like a delivery date or a wait time. Check how often you beat it, hit it and miss it.
